etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English sour, from Old English sūr (“sour”), from Proto-West Germanic *sūr, from Proto-Germanic *sūraz (“sour”), from Proto-Indo-European *súHros (“sour”).

Cognate with West Frisian soer, Dutch zuur (“sour”), Low German suur, German sauer (“sour”), Danish, Swedish and Norwegian sur, French sur (“sour”), Faroese súrur (“sour”), Icelandic súr (“sour, bitter”), Polish ser (“cheese”), Czech sýr (“cheese”), Slovak syr (“cheese”), Russian сырой (syroj, “raw”), Ukrainian сири́й (syrýj, “raw”), Old Church Slavonic сꙑръ (syrŭ, “moist, cheese”).

definitions.definition: Tasting of acidity.

quote.citation: 1627 (indicated as 1626), Francis [Bacon], “(please specify the page, or |century=I to X)”, in Sylua Syluarum: Or A Naturall Historie. In Ten Centuries. […], London:  […]  William Rawley […]; [p]rinted by J[ohn] H[aviland] for William Lee […], →OCLC:
quote.text: All sour things, as vinegar, provoke appetite.

quote.citation: 2018 May 16, Adam Rogers, “The Fundamental Nihilism of Yanny vs. Laurel”, in Wired:
quote.text: A few types of molecules get sensed by receptors on the tongue. Protons coming off of acids ping receptors for "sour." Sugars get received as "sweet." Bitter, salty, and the proteinaceous flavor umami all set off their own neural cascades.

definitions.definition: Made rancid by fermentation, etc.
Tasting or smelling rancid.
(of a person's character) Hostile or unfriendly.

quote.citation: c. 1591–1592 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Third Part of Henry the Sixt, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene i]:
quote.text: He was a scholar  […]  / Lofty and sour to them that loved him not, / But to those men that sought him sweet as summer.

definitions.definition: Excessively acidic and thus infertile. (of soil)
Containing excess sulfur. (of petroleum)
Unfortunate or unfavorable.

quote.citation: 1613 (date written), William Shakespeare, [John Fletcher], “The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eight”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene ii]:
quote.text: Let me embrace thee, sour adversity

quote.citation: 2011 October 1, Phil Dawkes, “Sunderland 2 - 2 West Brom”, in BBC Sport‎[1]:
quote.text: The result may not quite give the Wearsiders a sweet ending to what has been a sour week, following allegations of sexual assault and drug possession against defender Titus Bramble, but it does at least demonstrate that their spirit remains strong in the face of adversity.

definitions.definition: (music) Off-pitch, out of tune.

quote.citation: 2010, Aniruddh D. Patel, Music, Language, and the Brain, page 201:
quote.text: Unlike what the name implies, there is nothing inherently wrong with a sour note: It is perfectly well-tuned note that would sound normal in another context (and which presumably would not sound sour to someone unfamiliar with tonal music).

definitions.definition: The sensation of a sour taste.
A drink made with whiskey, lemon or lime juice and sugar.
(by extension) Any cocktail containing lemon or lime juice.
A sweet/candy having a sharply sour taste.

quote.citation: 2022, Michael N. Riley, ARCH BOOK I, page 78:
quote.text: “You know I like them candies, especially the lemon sours.”

definitions.definition: A sour or acid substance; whatever produces a painful effect.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto III”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: For many Years of Sorrow can dispense; A Dram of Sweet is worth a Pound of Sour

definitions.definition: The acidic solution used in souring fabric.
(transitive) To make sour.
(intransitive) To become sour.

quote.citation: 1720, Jonathan Swift, To Stella, on transcribing my Poems:
quote.text: So the sun's heat, with different powers, / Ripens the grape, the liquor sours.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To spoil or mar; to make disenchanted.

quote.citation: 1611 April (first recorded performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Cymbeline”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene v]:
quote.text: To sour your happiness I must report, / The queen is dead.

quote.citation: 1749, Henry Fielding, The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling, volume (please specify |volume=I to VI), London: A[ndrew] Millar, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: He was prudent and industrious, and so good a husbandman, that he might have led a very easy and comfortable life, had not an arrant vixen of a wife soured his domestic quiet.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To become disenchanted.
(transitive) To make (soil) cold and unproductive.

quote.citation: 1832, Joseph Harrison, Sir Joseph Paxton, The Horticultural Register, page 396:
quote.text: stagnant water , which tends to sour the soil

definitions.definition: To macerate (lime) and render it fit for plaster or mortar.
(transitive) To process (fabric) after bleaching, using hydrochloric acid or sulphuric acid to wash out the lime.
